content:
Less than two months after President Donald Trump called Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed a “RADICAL Extremist, Terrorist Sympathizer,” the president is now praising him as a “smart guy.”

As El-Sayed continues to push for Medicare for All, he publicly suggested “TrumpCare” as the potential name for the policy. Trump complimented El-Sayed in an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday and called the idea of adding his name to the universal healthcare proposal “very smart.”

“I know I’ll be meeting with him,” Trump said. “Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go.” Trump also said that he and the newly elected Democrats in Congress could do “great things together.”

On Saturday, Trump shared a screenshot of El-Sayed’s mock-up of a gold TrumpCare insurance card on Truth Social, days after El-Sayed had advocated for Trump to reconsider Medicare for All.

“Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed captioned the image on Nov. 12. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

This series of events marks a notable shift from the politicians’ earlier comments. Throughout the midterm election, El-Sayed and Trump openly criticized ea ch other. El-Sayed called Trump “an idiot” on Hasan Minhaj’s podcast. Trump called El-Sayed, who is Muslim, an “extremist” and “radical” whose win would be “a devastating blow to our country” and told voters at a Florida rally to “send him back to where he came from.” (El-Sayed was born and raised in Michigan.)

El-Sayed’s campaign team did not respond to HuffPost’s request for comment to clarify whether a meeting had actually been set between the two, though Vice President JD Vance’s office confirmed on Sunday that it had already reached out to arrange a meeting with the incoming senator. The White House referred HuffPost back to the president’s original statements when asked for comment.

What Trump’s Latest About-Face Could Mean, According To Political Experts

Roderick Hart, professor emeritus of communications at the University of Texas and author of “Trump and Us: What He Says and Why People Listen,” argued that Trump seems to love to be hyperbolic when it comes to attacking enemies, until the enemies win.

“I think he likes winners and he doesn’t really care what the game is,” Hart told HuffPost. “I don’t know that Trump admires anyone other than himself, but I think he comes close to admiring winners of all sorts. … He likes really, really successful people.”

The switch from attacking El-Sayed during the election to praising him mirrors how the president formerly treated — and now treats — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani after he was elected in 2025.

“Trump has always shown himself to be somewhat of an opportunist politically, where I don’t think he’s really steeped in ideology,” said Khaled Beydoun, a professor at Arizona State University College of Law. “So when Mamdani won, it really came as no surprise that [Trump] was going to veer in [Mamdani’s] direction. And that’s the same for El-Sayed too.”

I think he likes winners and he doesn’t really care what the game is. I don’t know that Trump admires anyone other than himself, but I think he comes close to admiring winners of all sorts.

- Roderick Hart, author of “Trump and Us: What He Says and Why People Listen”

It could be Trump’s attempt to establish a political presence on the left since Democrats are now the majority, but Beydoun argues Trump is not that loyal to traditional Republican values and cares more about his own standing.

“Medicare for All is inimical to the broader agenda of the Republican Party, but he’s not somebody who is loyal or allegiant to the broader Republican Party,” Beydoun said. “So if he feels as if meeting with El-Sayed, in the same way he met with Mamdani, and paying lip service to Medicare for All is going to bolster his individual profile and his individual interests, he’s going to do it.”

Trump’s recent obsession with his building projects has also suggested he is more focused on physical, permanent monuments reflecting his presidency than on legislative work. These proposed TrumpCare cards are physical items with his name on them.

“Trump is beginning to think about his life and his family name beyond his presidency and how it seems for the foreseeable future,” Beydoun said.

With Mamdani, too. The mayor and president announced building affordable housing in New York City with federal funding in September — more physical reflections of Trump being president that also benefit what Democrats are fighting for.

Appealing to Trump’s vanity is a familiar playbook for leaders trying to win him over, said Robert Rowland, a rhetoric professor at the University of Kansas. Rowland pointed to French President Emmanuel Macron and NATO’s Mark Rutte as examples, both of whom have praised the president in the past.

“In the case of Macron and Rutte, they praise the president shamelessly, something that feeds President Trump’s ego and gives him the good publicity that he craves,” Rowland said. “El-Sayed’s proposal to name some form of Medicare for All after President Trump also appeals to Trump’s vanity and offers him the opportunity for creating a legacy.”

Hart said Trump recognizes flattery for what it is, even if he welcomes it.

“Trump is not stupid. He can certainly see the kind of cloying attempts by other people to work him,” he said. “But because his ego is so fragile, he can probably tell part of himself that this is good.”

For El-Sayed, engaging Trump without waiting for an apology over Trump’s campaign rhetoric is a calculated gamble, Beydoun said, particularly in Michigan, where a sliver of Arab and Muslim voters backed Trump in 2024. Even if universal healthcare has virtually no chance of passing, a high-profile sit-down gives both politicians something they want.

“One thing about Abdul is that he’s a very sophisticated operator, and he knows how to leverage messaging and strategize specific talking points to resonate with power,” Beydoun said. “Essentially what he’s doing here is he’s kind of painting Trump into a corner. … Even though you might have detractors to say, ‘Why is he working with somebody who’s vilified him as being a terrorist and a member of the Muslim Brotherhood?’ I think those who understand the way in which the political landscape in D.C. works see this as really smart.”

Beydoun pointed out that Mamdani also never received an apology from Trump after winning City Hall. El-Sayed therefore must recognize that waiting for one “has no utility,” Beydoun argued.

“The likelihood of [Medicare for All] happening is next to zero, but they’ll have a song and dance, they’ll meet at the Oval Office, have a press conference, a dog and pony show,” Beydoun said. “I think it’ll benefit both of them in different ways.”

Still, Hart cautioned that Trump’s “warmth” is never guaranteed to last.

“I think Trump, he lives in the moment,” Hart said. “[Supporters] don’t know from moment to moment who they’re working for... [Trump] could turn on a dime tomorrow and lambaste El-Sayed for being a communist. Nobody should assume [this is] the end of the story.”
